title: The Navajo Code Talkers
text:
In 1942 the US Marine Corps needed a way to send battlefield messages by radio that the Japanese could not read, and that could be sent and decoded faster than with cipher machines. Philip Johnston, a civil engineer who had grown up on the Navajo reservation as a missionary's son, suggested the Navajo language, which was unwritten, very complex and spoken by almost no outsiders.

The first group of twenty-nine Navajo recruits built the code themselves. They chose Navajo words for military terms: a dive bomber was a chicken hawk, a submarine an iron fish, a tank a tortoise. For other words, each letter of the English alphabet had several Navajo words. Then they memorized it all; nothing was carried in writing in combat. Many of these men had gone to government boarding schools where they had been punished for speaking Navajo.

The program grew to several hundred code talkers, who served with Marine units across the Pacific. At Iwo Jima in 1945, according to the signal officer Major Howard Connor, six code talkers worked around the clock during the first two days and sent more than 800 messages without error. He later said that without the Navajos the Marines would never have taken the island.

The code was never broken. It stayed classified until 1968, so the code talkers could not speak of their work for years. In 2001 the original twenty-nine received the Congressional Gold Medal.
lesson: A team gains its edge from differences others overlook. Knowledge and skills that seem marginal can become the team's greatest strength.
people: Navajo Marines, Philip Johnston, Howard Connor
location: Pacific theater, including Iwo Jima, Japan
source: US Marine Corps records; Sally McClain, Navajo Weapon (1994)
